analysis.title: Zoomer Boom: Why the Youth Job Market Is Stronger Than It Looks
key_insights: Youth unemployment fell to 9.3% in October 2026, among the lowest readings in recent decades, despite worries that AI is hurting young workers' job prospects.

The gap between youth and overall unemployment normalized to 5.2 percentage points in October, after a worrying upward trend through 2025 tied to Liberation Day tariffs, policy uncertainty and early corporate AI use.
In the last 40 years there have been very few periods with youth unemployment below 10%, so the youth labor market is tight in historical context.
The Gen Z cohort is large, with births peaking at 4.3 million in 2007, a US record. The labor market is taking time to absorb it, which may explain the perception of a difficult market.
Youth labor force participation peaked at 56.9% in February 2023 and fell to 54.4% in August 2025. The youth labor force shrank by 627,000 while youth population rose by nearly half a million.
College enrollment share of the youth population rose from 44.7% in 2023 to an estimated 48.8% in 2025, about 1.8 million more students, which explains part of the participation drop.
Participation recovered sharply to 55.5%, with a seasonally adjusted 653,000 young people entering the labor force from August to October 2026.
MIM raised its headline CPI forecast to 3.9% for 2026 and 2.3% for 2027, citing uncertainty around resolution of the Iran conflict and lingering effects of high prices.
MIM expects a 25-bp Fed hike in December and another in Q1 2027, after the October inflation report and a stronger-than-expected payrolls number.
Risks include Iran-driven oil swings, scrutiny and possible political limits on AI capex, and a consumer pullback if AI-related equity valuations collapse.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Historically low, signaling a tight youth labor market and supporting the case for a firm labor backdrop.
Normalized gap suggests youth stress has eased relative to the broader labor market.
Sharp rebound from 54.4% low in August 2025 adds labor supply and may temper wage pressure.
Elevated 2026 inflation tied to Iran conflict and high prices supports further Fed tightening.
Implies a December 25-bp hike and another in Q1 2027 from 3.75% at end of 2025.
Steady growth forecast despite oil and AI capex risks.
Down from 4.4% at end of 2025, consistent with a firm labor market.

risk_factors: Iran conflict and sharp oil price swings could change forecasts.
Firms struggle with higher costs even if oil is stable at a higher level, a growth risk if labor markets and consumers falter.
Scrutiny of AI capex and new Congress governance policies could slow data center investment, with risks of a sharper decline now elevated.
Hyperscalers guide for higher 2027 capex, and market appetite for more data center funding is uncertain.
Collapse in AI-related equity valuations could hurt consumption and growth.

tension_points.bull_case: Youth unemployment at 9.3% is historically low, the gap to overall unemployment is a benign 5.2 points, and 653,000 young people entered the labor force from August to October 2026.
tension_points.bear_case: AI adoption and a low-hire, low-fire market make job finding harder, and participation fell to 54.4% in August 2025 as many Gen Z delayed entry into the workforce.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A renewed rise in youth unemployment or a reversal of the participation recovery from 55.5%, especially if consumers falter or AI-related equity valuations collapse.

theme_stances.key_argument: Youth unemployment is historically low and participation is recovering, so the youth job market is stronger than perceived.
theme_stances.evidence: the youth labor market appears to be strengthening

theme_stances.key_argument: October inflation and strong payrolls set the stage cleanly for a December hike, with another in Q1 2027.
theme_stances.evidence: We continue to expect a 25-bp hike in December
